MINISTERS' SALARIES AND MEMBERS' INDEMNITIES

speakeroldname: Mr. HARRY LEADER (Portage la Prairie) moved:
speechtext:
That, in view of the rigid necessity for economy in all walks of public and private life, it is incumbent upon this parliament to give the country a lead in this matter, and therefore, in the opinion of this House the government should take steps to reduce the indemnities and salaries paid to ministers of the Crown, the leader of the Opposition, members of the Senate and members of the House of Commons by 12j per cent of the present indemnities and salaries.
He said: I had no intention of letting this resolution drop, but it is perfectly obvious that under the present circumstances, in view of the lateness of the hour, it will not come to a vote this afternoon. I understand that according to the rules of the House if the resolution is not voted on by six o'clock it automatically falls to the last place among the motions, and that might involve the danger of its not being taken up again this year. I certainly do not wish to withdraw the resolution, but I fear this danger; and at this stage, although the subject is one of the greatest importance, I will cut my remarks short if the House is willing to let the matter come to a vote.
Explain.
Oh, oh.

I am sure that hon. members wish to give me a fair show. I know that this resolution is out of the ordinary. A motion of this complexion is not usual in the House; resolutions of this kind usually ask for an increase in indemnities. That is what we have been used to.
Oh, no.

Back on the farm I always thought it was hardly a square deal when I read of resolutions being introduced into parliament asking for increases in indemnities of $200 or $300. When I hire a man for $50 I do not expect him to ask for $75, after he has agreed to the wage I offer. In proposing this resolution, Mr. Speaker, I hope I have the goodwill of hon. members.
Hear, hear. [DOT]

I expected that. But if some gentlemen choose to disagree with me I trust that my honesty of purpose will not be questioned and that it will be taken for granted that I am actuated by a desire faithfully to serve those whom I represent.
The necessity for economy and retrenchment is apparent to all hon. members. I believe the government are fairly well seized of the necessity of rigid economy in administration and are working with that end in view. To some extent, however, as I see it, they are handicapped by the taunt, and rightly so, that while they are willing to economize on the other fellow, they still cling to the higher indemnities voted to members and ministers in 1920. Economy is the crying need of the hour. While there are men who by the advantage of birth or sheer ability are not forced by circumstances to curtail their expenditure, the fact remains that the great body of the people are forced to economize.
The Speech from the Throne declared the need for economy. The amendment and the subamendment thereto stressed this need. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I believe that in adopting this resolution we would give a practical demonstration of sincerity in our demand for economy. In my opinion this is the final test. The amount that we would save is perhaps not very large, in fact it is a mere bagatelle as we count'money here in Ottawa, but I think the people would rather have a small surplus than a huge deficit.
Briefly, what this resolution means is to cut $500 off the indemnity of each member of this House, $500 off the indemnity of each member of the Senate, and $1,750 off the salary of each minister of the Crown, thereby saving approximately $200,000 a year. But the monetary saving is of the least importance. I maintain that the principle is a veiy large one and places the government and members in an unassailable position from which to effect economies of a like nature. The burden of salary reductions generally falls upon those who are least able to bear it. Let me illustrate. I remember reading about two years
Members' Indemnities

ago an award respecting the wages of men engaged in the packing plants in Chicago. By that award the first class men, those getting the highest wages, were to receive a reduction of 2i cents an hour; the second class men, those getting lower wages, were to receive a reduction of 5 cents per hour; and the third class men, those in every instance least able to bear the decrease, were to receive a reduction of 7i cents per hour. I repeat, the burden of reduced wages generally falls upon those least able to bear it.
I would not for a moment reduce the salaries of those who are only receiving sufficient for a decent livelihood, but I would urge upon the government to go after the higher paid officials, for instance, the higher paid judiciary. We all admire and respect very much our Minister of Justice (Sir Lomer Gouin), and it is not in a spirit of antipathy towards him that I make these remarks. But I feel that along this line we might perhaps save considerable expenditure. I have extracted some figures from the speech made last session by the hon. member for Laprairie and Napierville (Mr. Lanctot), and I would ask his pardon if I have encroached on his rights; I think not, however. These figures are in reference to a judge who was a Minister of the Crown, and I quote them to show what he received from the public treasury. He received as salary, 878,147.50-
In how many years?
As a state pensioner-I shall have something to say about pensions- he received $70,893.33. I think there must be added to that two or three years' pension at ' $4,606.66 per year.
He is still living.

And drawing a pension. He received travelling expenses as a judge to the amount of $282.90. While a member of parliament he received in indemnities $40,555. As Minister of Justice he received $76,636.20. For travelling expenses as a Minister of the Crown he received $3,196.25. For trips to Europe during the war he received $9,000. When he came back he was offered a job-that is the way I would put it-as counsel of the Labrador commission and was paid in advance $5,000. I do not know whether he ever started work on this job, but that is the sum he was paid in advance.	.
Would the hon. member go on the Labrador coast for so small a salary?
Order.
How could he get wealthy if he was not paid?

Mr. Speaker, conditions in Canada to-day, while not as bad as in soma other countries, are bad enough. We have in western Canada public schools closed for want of funds. Premier Bracken, according to a newspaper report, is authority for the statement that there are $14,000,000 of unpaid taxes in my province of Manitoba. Now a new method is being adopted there to collect taxes. Hitherto the authorities

Members' Indemnities
were satisfied to take a man's land or house and sell it for taxes. Now they are going to garnishee the wages of the defaulter. I feel, Mr. Speaker, that. owing to these conditions, we should share a little of this burden.
The question arises, then: Is there room for economy in our administration? In that connection let me read an article published in the London Free Press-and this will be my only quotation. I am not fully conversant with the conditions in eastern Canada with which this newspaper comment deals, but they are no doubt similar to those in the West. It says:
Aie we over-governed in Canada? We have only eight to nine million people and yet we have a federal parliament and 9 legislatures. The total population of the Maritime provinces is slightly over a million people and yet they have 3 legislative assemblies, 3 lieutenant-governors, 3 speakers and in all three provinces the paraphernalia of the mother of parliaments. Nova Scotia, in addition to a. legislative assembly of 43 members, also has the luxury of an Upper House with 21 members. Prince Edward Island, with a population less than Middlesex county, has all the fuss and feathers of a real parliament. It has a legislature of 30 members, with a sessional indemnity of $500 each, and a cabinet of 8 although only 4 are paid. New Brunswick has a house of 48 members, drawing an indemnity of $1,000 per session, and a premier and 6 cabinet ministers.

Will the hon. member
permit a question?
Yes.
The other night the hon. member raised a question as to who was the representative of Portage la Prairie. Why not divide the indemnity between the two members concerned?

I may tell the hon. gentleman that I have no doubt as to who represents Portage la Prairie, although some may have. It is evident from the article I have read, therefore, that the impression is abroad that we are over-governed in Canada.

If the hon. gentleman will permit me a question, I wonder if before he leaves his interesting financial details he would give us the expenditure of the Ontario government in law fees during the last few years. My recollection is that it runs to $600,000.

I regret that I cannot
answer the hon. gentleman's question. I believe there is extravagance in administration and that we could avoid some of that extravagance. I would like just for a moment to make a comparison of the cabinet of the United States with that of Canada. The United States cabinet comprises ten ministers, each with a salary of $12,000 per year, so that it costs the United States $120,000 for their 74
cabinet. In Canada we have seventeen ministers with salaries of $14,000 a year each, the total cost being $238,000, or almost double what it costs the United States with twelve times as many people.

Is not the difference in
number between the United States and Canadian cabinets explained by differences in constitutional status?

That may be, but if the
Canadian ministers could show us the surplus that the United States ministers are showing we would be willing to pay them the bigger salary. I am quite sure that the members of the United States cabinet are carrying on their work to the satisfaction of the American people, at the salaries they are receiving.
Would my hon. friend
I would ask hon. members to be fair toward the hon. member who has the floor.

Now, let us compare our
representation with that of the United States. As I have pointed out, the United States has twelve times as many people as we have. Canada will have 245 representatives in the House of Commons after the next election; the United States has 435 members in its House of Representatives. It is true that the United States indemnity per representative is $7,500 while that of the Canadian representative is only $4,000. But the unit of representation in the United States is 210.000 while in Canada it is a little over 36,000. You can therefore see that we have at least six representatives where the United States has one, and that where it costs us $24,000. at $4,000 per year, the cost to the United States is only $7,500. A comparison could also be made with Australia, where there are 75 representatives with a population 35 per cent less than that of Canada. We might also make a comparison with England, where the unit of representation is 70,000. I think, therefore, it is fairly established that our administration is extravagant. The United States Senate has 96 members, or one senator for every 1,000,000 inhabitants, while the Canadian Senate has about 10 senators for every 1,000,000 people. In Australia I believe they have about half as many senators as representatives, so the comparison with Australia is very striking indeed.
Our administration is too costly; there should be a reduction, and I believe the people generally are waking up to that fact. Nova Scotia last year reduced the sessional indemnity from $1,500 to $1,000. Alberta is also effecting a reduction in indemnity thi*



Members' Indemnities
year; I forget the exact figures, but I believe the reduction is from $2,000 to $1,800. A bill has passed the Manitoba legislature this session reducing the sessional indemnity of members of the legislature from $1,800 to $1,500 per annum. It is evident therefore, that the people are realizing that something must be done along this line, and the purpose of this resolution is to draw the attention of hon. members to the fact that it is our move.
If we accept this cut in our indemnity, we can more than compensate for the loss in money by economy in time. I have been here only a short time, but in my judgment the sessions could be shortened very materially by the co-operation of all groups in expediting the work of parliament. I have no ground for complaint this year; we are moving along much faster than last. For instance, while it took fifteen days to dispose of the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne last year, the time occupied this year was only nine days, and no one doubts that the work was just as effectively done. Moreover, the speeches are much shorter and a great deal better. Another reason why I believe we can save time is found in the fact that the hon. member for St. John city (Mr. Baxter), speaking for his party, I presume, declared a willingness to co-operate with the government in an endeavour to save the time of the House. I believe this can be done, and speaking as a farmer I know it would mean a great deal to western members if we could get through our work in time to superintend our seeding operations at home. I would not for a moment suggest a shirking of our responsibility as representatives of the people; I rather suggest that we concentrate on our duties and perform them with the utmost despatch.
I think that the House should accept this resolution. In effecting a reduction of $500 in the sessional indemnity the amputation might be somewhat painful, but we would all feel much better after the operation. I would point out also that it is not money alone that induces men to go into public life; in fact, we get quite the contrary impression as we listen to the speeches of members when they learn that they have been elected to represent the people in parliament. I question if there is an hon. member in this House who did not on the night of his election say something to this effect: "Ladies and gentlemen, from the bottom of my heart I thank you for the honour you have done me." I remember the right hon. member for Grenville (Mr. Meighen), who was the member for Portage la Prairie, when he was assured of his election for the first time, saying to us: "Ladies and gentlemen, this is the proudest moment

of my life thus far." It Was such a catchy phrase that I used it myself when the occasion arose. I intended to make some further remarks, but I see it is almost six o'clock. I earnestly commend this resolution to the attention of the House and I hope that hon. members will see their way clear to voting for it.
